intro: Instead of a scherzo, Brahms writes a C minor song in three beats. Trumpets and timpani remain silent while the melody passes between the strings and solo winds.
question: What changes when a melody returns in a different colour?

sections.label: Opening song returns · approximate
sections.mNote: horn takes the cello melody; cellos add an upward arpeggio

relations.label: The C minor song returns
relations.basis: The ternary movement restores its opening song after the middle section, with changed scoring; the matched phrases lie inside the opening A and the A′ section marked near 214 s. CENS diagonal mean 0.937, sustained 30 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 218.5 s (cache/form/brahms-3-poco-allegretto.txt, candidate 1; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: A song in three
cues.text: Brahms gives this movement a three-beat measure rather than a fast scherzo’s pace. Follow the long melodic phrases against the smaller movements of the accompaniment; their points of arrival need not coincide.
cues.evidence: The movement’s score is in 3/8 and marked Poco allegretto. This describes its recurring phrasing, not a timed instrumental entrance.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Follow the smaller swell
cues.text: Through these early phrases, notice how a local swell relaxes without becoming a full orchestral outburst. Keep attending to the accompaniment when the melody holds a note.
cues.evidence: The analysis shows a rise and fall in relative level around 0:30–0:45. It supports a local swell but does not separate melody from accompaniment.

cues.title: A summer in Wiesbaden
cues.text: Brahms wrote the Third Symphony in Wiesbaden in the summer of 1883. His First Symphony had reached performance in 1876, the Second in 1877; the Third followed six years later.
cues.evidence: Marc Mandel’s Boston Symphony programme note documents the composition in Wiesbaden and the earlier symphonies’ chronology. https://www.bso.org/works/brahms-symphony-no-3

cues.title: A contrasting interlude
cues.text: The central interlude works with shorter, repeated gestures rather than the opening melody’s long span. Listen across this stretch for a change of phrase length without expecting a sudden increase in force.
cues.evidence: Mandel describes the interlude’s repeated-note figure. The recording changes around 1:50–1:56, but its score position is only approximately located. https://www.bso.org/works/brahms-symphony-no-3
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Expansion and contraction
cues.text: Across this passage, the sound grows stronger and brighter before contracting again. Distinguish this brief expansion from the movement’s larger pattern of departure and return.
cues.evidence: The report shows a rise in relative level and high-frequency weight around 2:25–2:35, followed by a reduction around 2:40–2:45.

cues.title: Recognising a returning song
cues.text: In the later part of the movement, compare the familiar melody with its opening presentation. Brahms changes who carries the line; the notes can remain recognisable while their attack and sustaining colour change.
cues.evidence: Mandel documents the melody’s changing instrumental assignments. The approximate return region follows the score’s form and a recorded change near 3:34, not a verified horn entrance. https://www.bso.org/works/brahms-symphony-no-3
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: No trumpets or drums
cues.text: Throughout this movement, Brahms keeps trumpets and timpani silent. Listen for variety within that restricted ensemble: a familiar melody can change colour without acquiring percussion or a trumpet fanfare.
cues.evidence: The absence of trumpets and drums is a whole-movement scoring fact documented by Mandel, not an inference from the audio analysis. https://www.bso.org/works/brahms-symphony-no-3

cues.title: Vienna, December 1883
cues.text: Hans Richter conducted the Vienna Philharmonic in the premiere on 2 December 1883. All four movements end quietly; this movement’s restrained close belongs to a pattern that extends across the symphony.
cues.evidence: Mandel’s Boston Symphony note gives the premiere and identifies the quiet endings of all four movements. https://www.bso.org/works/brahms-symphony-no-3

cues.title: A fuller late statement
cues.text: In this late stretch, compare the stronger, brighter sound with the preceding quieter phrases. An increase in weight can enlarge a melody’s presentation without changing its contour.
cues.evidence: Relative level and high-frequency weight increase around 5:05–5:20 compared with 4:50–4:55. The measurement does not establish which instruments cause the change.

cues.title: One swell, then quiet
cues.text: The closing passage makes a substantial swell before withdrawing. Listen across the whole ending rather than treating its strongest point as the final chord: the release is part of the phrase.
cues.evidence: The highest five-second relative-level window occurs around 5:50; the recording then falls markedly through 5:55–6:05. This is a broad contour, not an aligned cadence time.

transitions.title: A cadence loses its downbeat
transitions.how: The song reaches a C minor cadence; an A♭ minor chord follows inside the same bar, before the ear can settle. Held wind chords then cross the bar lines, making upbeats sound like downbeats without changing the written 3/8. A♭ minor alternates with A♭ major, while the cellos’ syncopated line falls from A♭ towards E♭. The long melody gives way to repeated-note gestures: harmony and displaced accent, rather than a faster tempo, make the interlude different.
transitions.evidence: The approximate middle-section boundary is 1:50; analysis marks changes at 1:50 and 1:56, with lower level and brightness. The C minor cadence, following A♭ minor chord and displaced wind/cello writing are described at bars 49–61 in Kelly Dean Hansen’s score guide: http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus90.html. Its recording times are not used here.

transitions.title: Three notes find their home
transitions.how: Brahms brings back the song before bringing back its whole phrase. Clarinet and bassoon try its three-note opening in A♭ minor, then B♭ minor, over shifting chromatic string chords. The rising sequence finally reaches C minor, and the fragment’s note values lengthen. A solo horn then takes the melody formerly given to cellos; the freed cellos add an upward arpeggio beneath it. The return therefore grows from an altered fragment rather than arriving after an unrelated bridge.
transitions.evidence: The map places the return near 3:34; the analysis has a boundary there and a quiet C-minor region from 3:30. Hansen’s guide identifies the sequential thematic pickups and chromatic string harmonies at bars 93–98, then the horn reprise at bar 99: http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus90.html. The provisional relation confirms later matching phrases, not the horn’s entrance time.

transitions.title: The interlude’s chords become an ending
transitions.how: After the returning song’s C minor cadence, Brahms recalls the wind chords held across the bar line that once led into the interlude. This time their A♭ minor colouring does not open another middle section: fragments of the song redirect the harmony towards C minor. Strings join the displaced chords, and a diminished seventh intensifies the last swell. Longer note values briefly suggest 3/4 across the written 3/8 before the final tonic restores the smaller beat.
transitions.evidence: The closing-passage marker is 5:30, a measured boundary with a marked fall in level; the final swell follows around 5:45–5:50. The coda’s recalled cross-bar chords, diminished seventh and implied 3/4 are written features at bars 150–163, detailed in Hansen’s guide: http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus90.html. The map is not a bar alignment.

composer.background:
Brahms was born in Hamburg, the son of a professional musician, Johann Jakob Brahms, who played several instruments, and Christiane Nissen, a seamstress. His father supplied an introduction to practical music-making; Otto Friedrich Willibald Cossel and Eduard Marxsen gave him systematic piano and composition lessons. The young Brahms played for income and learned the trade from inside, accompanying, arranging and performing. Marxsen’s teaching connected keyboard technique with the study of Bach, Mozart and Beethoven. Those composers supplied working materials: Brahms’s later scores are full of old procedures subjected to new rhythmic pressure.

In 1853 he toured with the Hungarian violinist Ede Reményi and met Joseph Joachim, who became a lifelong collaborator. Joachim sent him to Robert and Clara Schumann in Düsseldorf. Robert’s article “Neue Bahnen”, published that October, announced the twenty-year-old as a major new figure before his music was widely available. The endorsement opened publishers’ doors and imposed an awkward expectation of scale. His early piano sonatas, already orchestral in weight and contrast, could be treated as promises of symphonies he had not yet written. Brahms responded by publishing selectively and destroying much of the work he did not wish to preserve.
composer.epithet: A composer who made a small interval generate a large form, and let conflicting rhythms keep a familiar melody unsettled.
